title: From profit to cash: reading the quality of earnings
subtitle: Four adjusting lines, and the ratio that says whether profit turns into money
openingQuestion: A company has net profit of VND 100bn but operating cash flow of only VND 30bn. How do you read that?
openingOptions: Normal, these two numbers are always different
Most of the profit has not turned into cash
The company is certainly falsifying its figures
Large depreciation in the period was deducted from profit
explanation: The two numbers differing is normal, but a gap of three times has to be explainable. There are only a few possible sources: depreciation and other non-cash items, changes in working capital, and one-off items. Depreciation is added back, which makes cash flow HIGHER than profit, so it cannot explain a shortfall in this direction. A shortfall almost always sits in working capital - receivables swelling because more was sold on credit, or inventory rising because goods are not moving. That is not yet fraud, but it is a question you have to answer before you trust the profit figure.

diagram.label: Add back depreciation and non-cash items

realWorldExample.description: An industry paid by milestone, with slow sign-off, routinely books profit long before the money arrives, so a low cash-flow-to-profit ratio is a feature of the sector rather than a warning sign. The same ratio at a retail chain that takes cash at the till is a different matter entirely - there, the money should arrive faster than the profit.

quiz.question: Under the indirect method, the starting point for calculating operating cash flow is:
options: Net revenue in the period
Net profit after tax
Cash at period start
EBITDA for the period
quiz.explanation: Operating cash flow, abbreviated OCF, starts from net profit and then adjusts for non-cash items and working capital. Revenue is too high up the income statement to have absorbed costs yet, EBITDA has already stripped out items the reconciliation needs to add back itself, and opening cash is a balance, not a flow.

quiz.question: Why is depreciation added back when working from net profit to operating cash flow?
options: Because depreciation is income, not an expense
Because depreciation is only a bookkeeping entry, always ignored
Because it reduces profit without any cash going out
To offset the cash spent buying the fixed assets
quiz.explanation: D&A is depreciation and amortisation, an accounting charge that does not send cash out of the door in the period. So on the way from net profit to operating cash flow it is added back. It is not ignored - it is a real cost of using up an asset - and the cash for that asset left the business earlier, in investing cash flow.

quiz.question: Receivables rise by VND 50bn during the period. How does that affect operating cash flow?
options: +VND 50bn: receivables rose, so operating cash flow rose with them
+VND 25bn: only half the increase is counted
No effect on operating cash flow this period
−VND 50bn: the revenue is booked, the cash has not arrived
quiz.explanation: A rise in receivables means the business has booked the revenue but not yet collected the money. Because no cash came in, operating cash flow falls. The sign is the trap: the receivable is an asset going up, which feels positive, but it is money sitting with the customer rather than in the account.

quiz.question: A company has net profit of VND 100bn but operating cash flow of negative VND 20bn. What does that signal?
options: A red flag: profit is booked but the cash never arrives
Normal, every business goes through periods like this
A sign the company is spending heavily on new fixed assets
A common thing during a phase of fast growth
quiz.explanation: Negative operating cash flow alongside positive profit is a red flag. The money may be stuck in receivables or inventory, or the way revenue is recognised may need a harder look. Capital spending would not do it, because that sits in investing cash flow, not operating - and growth explains a lag, not a negative.

quiz.question: What does negative financing cash flow usually mean?
options: The company is loss-making and is slowly draining the cash in its reserves
The company is repaying debt, buying back shares or paying dividends
The company cannot raise any capital from outside investors
The company is heading for bankruptcy within the short term
quiz.explanation: Financing cash flow, abbreviated CFF, records money tied to borrowing, issuing shares, dividends and buybacks. Negative CFF usually means the business is repaying debt or returning money to shareholders - which is often a sign of strength, not weakness. Losses show up in operating cash flow, not here.

keyTakeaways: Depreciation is added back and makes cash flow higher than profit; working capital is what drags it down
Rising receivables and inventory are deducted; rising payables are added back
An operating-cash-flow-to-net-profit ratio below 0.5x is a level where you go looking for the reason
The threshold depends on the industry: milestone payment is nothing like taking cash at the till

practicePrompt.question: Net profit VND 100bn, depreciation VND 40bn, receivables up VND 70bn, payables up VND 20bn, inventory unchanged. What is operating cash flow?
options: VND 90bn (= 100 + 40 − 70 + 20, signs correct)
VND 130bn (= 100 + 40 − 20 + 10, signs wrong)
VND 50bn (= 100 − 70 + 20, depreciation forgotten)
VND 210bn (= 100 + 40 + 70, receivables added)
practicePrompt.explanation: Depreciation is added back because it was deducted from profit without any cash leaving. A rise in receivables is SUBTRACTED, because the revenue is booked but the money is still with the customer. A rise in payables is ADDED, because the cost is booked but the cash has not left the account. So 100 + 40 − 70 + 20 = VND 90bn. The VND 50bn option forgets to add depreciation back - the most common slip. The VND 210bn option flips the sign on receivables, treating what a customer still owes as money already in.

summary.keyIdea: The gap between profit and cash has only a few possible sources, so it is always explainable - and whether it actually gets explained is the information
summary.formula: Operating cash flow ≈ Net profit + Depreciation − Rise in receivables − Rise in inventory + Rise in payables
summary.commonMistake: Treating a gap between profit and cash as simply how things are, without going looking for its source
summary.action: Take the last three years, work out operating cash flow over net profit, and see whether it is rising or falling

application.title: Work it out on a real set of accounts
application.message: Take net profit and operating cash flow for three consecutive years and divide one by the other. A low ratio in one year may be the cycle; low three years running is not.
application.secondary: If the ratio is drifting down while revenue is still growing, the next place to look is receivables and inventory.

sections.text: The three sections of the cash flow statement and why they are kept apart - that is covered in the lesson on what a cash flow statement is. This one is about using it: working from net profit down to operating cash flow, then reading the gap between the two numbers.

items: Add back depreciation and non-cash items: they were deducted from profit without a single dong leaving the account
Subtract the rise in receivables: the revenue is booked but the money is still with the customer
Subtract the rise in inventory: cash went out to buy the goods and the goods have not sold
Add the rise in payables: the cost is booked but not yet paid, so the money is still in the account

sections.text: The two middle lines are where the gap usually sits. A growing business almost always has receivables and inventory swelling along with revenue, so cash runs a beat behind profit - that is normal. What is not normal is revenue standing still while those two keep rising.

items: Above 1.2x: cash arrives faster than the profit is booked - typical of a model paid up front
Between 0.8x and 1.2x: most of the profit converts into cash, the normal range
Below 0.5x: cash is stuck in working capital, or there is something wrong with how revenue is recognised - go and find the reason

sections.label: The threshold depends on the industry
sections.text: A construction contractor paid by milestone has a low ratio as a feature of the sector, not as a warning sign. The same number at a retail chain taking cash at the till is a serious question. Compare the ratio against the business's own history and against competitors in the same industry, not against a universal threshold.

lines: Profit is an accounting opinion within a framework of standards; cash is the bank balance.
The gap between the two is always explainable - and whether it actually gets explained is the information.
